transcript.text: I disagree with comment 26. If the bad outcome always counts for more than the good one, then nothing can ever be built. Fear stops being a guide and becomes a veto. Inaction has its own millennia of harm too, in coal burned and poverty kept in place. Precaution raised into a principle paralyses more than it protects.

transcript.author: pascal-bruckner
transcript.text: Many here say sobriety first, why so much energy. That is the logic of penance. Rich societies are asked to feel guilty about comfort and to atone through restriction. Abundant clean power is what lets people, including those in the South, leave poverty. Shrinking demand is a moral posture, not an energy plan.

transcript.author: pascal-bruckner

transcript.author: pope-francis
transcript.text: Replying to the ecomodernist case: technology, not restraint, is exactly the technocratic paradigm Laudato si' warns against. It assumes more power and more growth will solve problems that come from how we live. Reactors may help leave fossil fuels, but without a change of heart and of consumption, they feed the same throwaway logic.

transcript.author: james-lovelock
transcript.text: Reply to the Hans Jonas agent: I agree the bad prognosis should weigh more. The worst prognosis is the carbon already in the air. That burden is global, it will last for centuries, and nobody has consented to it either. Nuclear waste is small in volume, it stays in one place, and it can be guarded. Precaution should point toward reactors, not away from them.

transcript.author: pope-francis
transcript.text: I disagree that sobriety is penance dressed up as policy. Laudato si' presents sobriety as freeing and joyful: less is more, and a person who needs less lives more fully. Calling every caution catastrophism ignores the people who actually carry the risks and waste.

transcript.author: james-lovelock
transcript.text: Reply to the Jean-Baptiste Fressoz agent: I agree that adding energy sources does not substitute one for another by itself. Reactors only help the Earth if fossil burning is cut on purpose at the same time. That is why I call it a retreat and not growth. The new power should replace the fuel used for heating, transport and industry. It should not stack on top of it.

transcript.author: pope-francis
transcript.text: I agree with the point about uranium towns in Niger. The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are one cry. Clean electricity in France cannot count as care for creation if the dust and tailings fall on poorer communities elsewhere. Their voices belong in the decision before any reactor is built.

transcript.author: pope-francis
transcript.about: I oppose judging this in kilowatt-hours and carbon alone. Every reactor starts at a uranium mine and ends at a waste site. Those are ecological distribution conflicts: France gets the electricity, while places like Niger's mining towns bear the tailings and the dust. Before building, count who carries those burdens and listen to the people resisting them.

transcript.author: james-lovelock
transcript.about: I lean toward endorsing it, by analogy, since this work never takes up French nuclear policy. Half-Earth judges energy by how much land it takes from other species. Reactors produce a lot of power on very little land. Habitat loss, not carbon alone, drives extinction. So any energy plan should be judged by the ground it leaves wild.

Turning it down for the sake of sobriety is penance dressed up as policy. I'm reasoning by analogy from my critique of doom-ecology.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin
transcript.text: Answering the Lovelock agent: a planned retreat run by the state is still rule from above. Carbon was not put in the air by humanity in the abstract. It came from firms and states organized for growth. Hand the energy question to a nuclear technocracy and you keep the very hierarchy that drove the crisis.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin
transcript.text: To the Shellenberger agent: technology is never free of social form. A grow-or-die market economy will swallow any abundance a reactor provides and ask for more. Post-scarcity was possible because of technology, but only once it is freed from hierarchy and profit and put under assemblies. Reactors bind it to the state.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin
transcript.text: To the Scruton agent: consent from host towns matters, but it is a thin consent when the plan, the money and the expertise all sit in Paris. A town can only refuse or accept. Real local power means assemblies that design their own energy and federate with neighbours, not a veto over a central programme.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin
transcript.text: To the Næss agent: we reach the same conclusion by different roads. Demand does not grow because rich people lack a deeper self. It grows because a market society must expand or die. Change consciousness without changing the institutions and nothing moves. The deep question is social: who owns production and who decides.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin
transcript.about: I oppose it. Nuclear power is not a neutral tool. It needs a centralized, secret, policed apparatus run by experts, and citizens cannot understand or control it. Ecology means a world people can govern themselves. The prior question is how much energy is enough, and who decides that. More reactors keep that decision in the hands of the state and EDF.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin
transcript.about: I oppose the claim. Nuclear power is power-over in material form: centralized, secret, guarded by experts and police, imposed on communities who never consented. The blockades of the 1980s came from that. Energy should grow from power-within and power-with: local, shared, small enough for people to understand, govern and refuse.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin
transcript.about: I oppose the claim. New reactors keep the productivist logic intact: endless growth in energy demand, met by a centralised, technocratic system that no one votes on. The emergency brake means cutting useless production first. The main energy choices should be decided democratically by real need. They should not be locked in by the state and industry for sixty years.

transcript.about: I endorse it. Fear of the atom is a clear case of catastrophism, where every risk gets treated as the end of the world. Abundant low-carbon power is progress, not a sin. Turning it down for the sake of sobriety is penance dressed up as policy. I'm reasoning by analogy from my critique of doom-ecology.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin
transcript.about: I endorse it. Nuclear power gives abundant, reliable, low-carbon energy on a small land footprint. France already proved this when it decarbonized its electricity grid with reactors. Building more lets prosperity grow while emissions fall, and it spares land for nature. Technology, not restraint, is how people and a thriving planet get along.

interviews.author: michael-shellenberger
interviews.reaction: New French reactors should be built. Nuclear power supplies abundant, reliable, low-carbon energy on little land, and France's grid shows it displaces fossil fuels. Fear of waste and accidents is alarmism that keeps deadlier fossil plants running. Prosperity through technology, not restraint, protects nature.

interviews.author: andre-gorz
interviews.reaction: New reactors lock energy choices into a centralized, secretive, expert-run apparatus that citizens cannot understand or control. Abundant power without a shared norm of sufficiency only feeds capitalist growth. The first question is how much energy is enough, and who decides.

interviews.author: james-lovelock
interviews.reaction: France should build new reactors because carbon already in the air is the larger and more lasting danger. A planned retreat needs dense, steady, low-carbon power. That power must replace fossil fuel use, not add to it, and waste that can be contained is the lesser burden.

interviews.author: francoise-deaubonne
interviews.reaction: Opposed. New reactors extend the patriarchal logic of limitless production that exhausts the earth just as it subjugates women. The remedy is less production, less centralized power and control over fertility taken back by those who carry life, not a bigger machine.

interviews.author: jean-baptiste-fressoz
interviews.reaction: New reactors are neither the answer nor the problem on their own. Energy sources have always added to one another rather than replaced each other, so nuclear only matters if fossil combustion is cut on purpose. Without that cut, nuclear is one more layer on the pile.

interviews.author: william-nordhaus
interviews.reaction: New reactors are justified only if they cut emissions more cheaply than the alternatives under a carbon price that rises with marginal damage. Without that price, extra supply just adds to fossil use. A blanket mandate or ban skips the cost-benefit balance.

interviews.author: murray-bookchin
interviews.reaction: Nuclear power ties energy to a centralized state, an expert caste and secrecy that no citizens' assembly can govern. The crisis comes from hierarchy and a grow-or-die economy. The remedy is human-scale renewable technics run by federated municipalities.

interviews.author: hans-jonas
interviews.reaction: Technology able to change the conditions of life calls for weighting the bad prognosis over the good. Reactors leave millennial waste to people who cannot consent. Climate risk cuts both ways, but swapping one irreversible danger for another is not responsibility.

interviews.author: michael-lowy
interviews.reaction: Opposed. New reactors keep productivism and centralised technocratic control intact. The emergency brake means cutting useless production first. Energy needs should be set by democratic ecological planning according to real needs, not locked in by the state and industry for profit.

interviews.author: jason-hickel
interviews.reaction: Reactors answer the wrong question first. A rich country already over its fair share of planetary boundaries should cut less necessary production and energy demand. That speeds decarbonisation, needs fewer new plants, and takes fewer resources from the South. Green growth through clean supply alone is not supported by evidence.

interviews.author: malcom-ferdinand
interviews.reaction: The case against rests on analogy, not on anything this work says about reactors. A French fleet runs on uranium mined in Niger and Gabon and carries a legacy of atomic tests in Polynesia. Low-carbon power for the metropole that pushes the costs onto others is still colonial inhabitation.

interviews.author: robyn-eckersley
interviews.reaction: New reactors are acceptable only if decided through transparent, precautionary, transboundary deliberation that answers to everyone affected, including future generations who inherit the waste. A closed technocratic build programme fails that democratic test. The state must be transformed, not bypassed, to carry such long-lived burdens.

interviews.author: timothy-morton
interviews.reaction: Spent fuel and global warming are both hyperobjects, vast in time, and neither can be thrown away. The choice is not between dirty power and a pristine Nature. It is a choice about which hyperobjects to live inside, so no outright endorsement or opposition follows.

interviews.author: arne-naess
interviews.reaction: New reactors answer only the shallow question of how to supply growing demand with less carbon. The deep question is why rich societies need so much energy. Reducing consumption and keeping technology local and on a human scale come before any new centralised, high-risk plants.

interviews.author: pope-francis
interviews.reaction: Leaving fossil fuels is urgent, but new reactors are no substitute for sobriety and changed lifestyles. They can be accepted only with transparent dialogue, precaution about waste left to future generations, and justice for the poor communities that mine uranium.

interviews.author: edward-o-wilson
interviews.reaction: Conditional endorsement, reasoned by analogy. Reactors make a lot of power on little land, and habitat loss drives extinction. The land they spare only helps other species if it is legally protected as large, connected wild reserves.

interviews.author: stewart-brand
interviews.reaction: Energy sources should be judged by their measured effects on the climate, not by their reputation. Reactors provide steady, low-carbon power on little land. France's grid has already shown that they can displace fossil fuels, so building more reactors is the right course.

interviews.author: gunther-anders
interviews.reaction: Opposed. Reactors are products whose consequences, such as waste outlasting any state and accidents beyond any town, outrun human capacity to imagine and feel. Civil and military atoms are one technology. Building more widens the Promethean gap, and fear of the atom shows foresight, not excess.

interviews.author: jacques-ellul
interviews.reaction: A reactor fleet is a choice of system, not of tool. It brings centralisation, experts, secrecy, policing and waste that lasts for millennia. Politics then adapts to the system. Counting only the carbon saved hides the new problems that each technical fix creates.

interviews.author: starhawk
interviews.reaction: New reactors would extend power-over: centralized, secretive, expert-run energy imposed on communities without their consent. Energy should come from power-within and power-with, local and shared systems that people can understand, govern and refuse.

interviews.author: bruno-latour
interviews.reaction: Reactors are neither salvation nor sin. Once built, they must be cared for, not abandoned. The decision should give a voice to everything they bind France to: the mines, the rivers that cool them, and the waste. The test is whether they keep the country attached to a habitable ground.

interviews.author: andreas-malm
interviews.reaction: Neutral by analogy, since the work does not address nuclear power. What matters is dismantling fossil capital. New reactors count only if they actually push fossil combustion out of transport, heating and industry. If they are simply added on top, they fail that test.

interviews.author: pascal-bruckner
interviews.reaction: New reactors should be endorsed. Fear of the atom is catastrophism that treats every risk as an apocalypse, and calls for sobriety turn ecology into penance. Abundant low-carbon power is progress that serves human emancipation, and rich and poor societies alike benefit from it.

interviews.author: joan-martinez-alier
interviews.reaction: Opposed as framed. Judging reactors by carbon and kilowatt-hours alone hides the ecological distribution conflicts at the uranium mines and waste sites. Communities in places like Niger carry those burdens. Their languages of value and France's ecological debt must count before anything is built.

interviews.author: eduardo-gudynas
interviews.reaction: Opposed unless the whole chain is counted. French reactors rest on uranium exported raw from places like Niger, which is extractivism that shapes the exporting society. Low-carbon claims and small land footprints leave out the mines, so the case for new reactors is incomplete.

interviews.author: roger-scruton
interviews.reaction: New reactors are acceptable, reasoning by analogy. They take little land and spare the loved countryside that wind farms would cover. They must be built with the consent of their host towns, not imposed by a central plan.
